messages.subject: Multiple trees
parts:
Hi all

I have another question. I am currently doing a Biog. ancestral area reconstruction in BioGeoBEARS. I was wondering if I should use several trees and summarize the info in a single tree for the ancestral area reconstruction (for example using trees generated from a bayesian analysis), however, I do not know if there is a way to do this in BioGeoBEARS. Currently I am using just one single tree for all my analyses, but I am not sure what is the best option.

Cheers!

messages.author: 665b3d97beb30882
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Multiple trees
parts:
Hi! It can be done fairly easily, you'd have to set up a
for-loop load a tree, run the analysis, store the result,
etc., for all trees.

Then run another for-loop to summarize over these results
against some reference tree (e.g. the BEAST consensus tree).

The only tricky bit is making sure which nodes go with which
nodes in the BEAST consensus tree. Every tree may have
different node numbers when read into R, and some trees will
lack nodes found in the consensus tree.

I've found the simplest thing is to take the consensus tree,
and for every node, make a list of the tip species. Then,
for each sampled tree, for each list of species, look for
the LCA node, check that it includes ONLY those species, and
if so, keep those probabilities.

At the end, average over all the probabilities for each node.

This won't be super-fast, because it's R, but it works. I
can say from experience that it is much easier to do this
than it is to read DIVA and LAGRANGE output files into R and
trying to summarize over those!

I debate about the "Bayes-DIVA" and "Bayes-LAGRANGE" type
strategies -- they aren't really Bayesian, more like
pseudo-Bayesian. And, as far as I can tell the results
usually aren't much different than if you just use the
probabilities on the BEAST maximum clade credibility consensus.

Actually, when DEC+J models are favored, I suspect that tree
topology will matter a lot more, since the key events are
those jump-dispersals at speciation.

Cheers!
Nick
